extracted.intended_audience: researchers, evaluators, and policymakers interested in peer review and research funding (scientometrics, research policy, funding agencies)
extracted.subtask_short: peer review evaluation of grant applications
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the peer review procedure for project-based grant applications in biology and medicine, with emphasis on reliability, fairness, and validity and on methodological approaches to study peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliability is one of the three primary criteria studied for peer review of grant applications; overall reliability is reported as fair (intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.41).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inter-rater reliability metrics (e.g., intraclass correlation coefficient) to quantify consistency of review outcomes; interpret discipline-specific variation (see disciplinary differences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) as reliability metric
rubrics_metrics.description: The study reports an intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) of 0.41 overall to quantify reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply ICC to measure overall agreement among reviewers; report ICC values and consider thresholds/interpretation (the paper describes 0.41 as 'fair').

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary differences in reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed sizeable differences in reliability between disciplines: biology (ICC = 0.45) versus medicine (ICC = 0.20).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating peer review reliability, analyze and report differences across disciplines or fields rather than assuming uniform reliability across domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness (absence of systematic bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fairness is assessed by testing potential sources of bias (gender, age, nationality, academic status of applicant, requested amount of funding, institutional surrounding); multiple logistic regression models found these potential sources of bias to be non-significant predictors of the funding decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate fairness by statistically testing whether applicant characteristics or institutional/contextual factors systematically predict funding outcomes; identify and report any such biases or their absence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity (predictive validity of funding decisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Validity is examined via bibliometric analysis, which provides evidence that the funding decisions of a public funding organization for basic project-based research are in line with the future publication success of applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess predictive validity by comparing funding outcomes to later objective performance indicators (e.g., publication output, citation impact) to determine whether funded applicants achieve greater subsequent research success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of scientific performance indicators in selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple logistic regression models reveal only scientific performance indicators as significant predictors of the funding decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider which applicant-level performance metrics (publication record, citation measures, prior productivity) actually predict funding decisions and report their effect sizes; use these indicators to understand selection mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological breadth and process-focused research
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper argues for an expansion of approaches and methodologies in peer review research by increasingly focusing on process rather than outcome and by including a more diverse set of methods (e.g., content analysis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond outcome metrics (reliability/fairness/validity), study the review process itself (arguments reviewers use, decision procedures, committee dynamics) using qualitative and mixed methods such as content analysis, process tracing, and ethnographic or case-study approaches.
